stages.title: Complete chess rules
stages.hook: You have only a king and a bishop left against a lone king. Can you ever win? The rules of chess have an answer, and it is not what most people guess.
explain: White always moves first, then the players take turns. You cannot pass. A game ends in one of three ways: checkmate (a win), resignation (a player gives up), or a draw.

A draw is a tie. There are several kinds. Stalemate is when the player to move is not in check but has no legal move. Players can also agree to a draw. A position repeated three times, or 50 moves by each side with no pawn move and no capture, can be claimed as a draw. If neither side has enough pieces to checkmate, such as king against king, the game is drawn too.

Good manners matter. Shake hands, do not talk during a game, and in serious play, if you touch a piece you must move it. Moves are written in algebraic notation: a letter for the piece (K, Q, R, B, N; none for pawns), then the square, so Nf3 means a knight goes to f3. An x shows a capture, + means check and # means checkmate.

example.q: Black has only a king on h8. White has a king on f7 and a queen on g6. It is Black's turn. What is the result?
steps: Is Black in check? The queen on g6 does not attack h8, and the king on f7 does not either. So no check.
Can the black king move? g8, g7 and h7 are all attacked by the white queen or king.
Not in check and no legal move is stalemate.

analogies.home: Stalemate is like a board game where you must move but every move is against the rules, so the game is called a tie.
analogies.city: A one-way traffic jam where no car can move is like a stalemate.
analogies.farm: A fox with no way to catch the hen and no safe step is stuck. Nobody wins.
analogies.sport: A match that ends level after both sides have no way to score is a draw.

stages.mnemonic: Check and no escape: mate. No check and no move: stalemate.
terms: Stalemate
The player to move is not in check but has no legal move. The game is a draw.
Draw
A game that ends in a tie.
Algebraic notation
The way moves are written down, like Nf3 or exd5.
Threefold repetition

misc.wrong: Stalemate is a win for the player who cannot move.
misc.right: Stalemate is a draw. Nobody wins.

stages.limits: Rules for time controls, touch-move and some draw claims differ a little between clubs, tournaments and online sites.

panel.why: A draw rewards defence, and checkmate must include a real attack.

teach.model: A game ends when a king is checkmated, a player resigns, or it is a draw. A draw can be a stalemate, an agreement, a repeated position or too few pieces. Moves are written down with letters and squares.

stages.title: Castling and en passant
stages.hook: There is one move in chess where two pieces move at once. And another where a pawn captures a pawn that is not on the square it lands on. What are they?
explain: Castling moves the king two squares towards a rook, and the rook jumps over to the other side of the king. It protects the king and wakes up the rook. Kingside castling is written O-O (king to g1, rook to f1 for White). Queenside castling is O-O-O (king to c1, rook to d1).
You may castle only if the king and that rook have never moved, there are no pieces between them, the king is not in check, and the king does not pass through or land on a square that is attacked.

En passant ("in passing") is a special pawn capture. If a pawn moves two squares from its start and lands beside an enemy pawn, that enemy pawn may capture it as if it had moved only one square. This must be done on the very next move or the chance is lost.

example.q: White pawn on e5. Black plays d7-d5, landing beside it. What can White do?
steps: The black pawn moved two squares and now stands next to the white pawn on the fifth rank.
White can capture it en passant, on the very next move.
The white pawn moves diagonally to d6 and the black pawn on d5 is removed: exd6.

analogies.home: Castling is like tucking a treasure into a safe and moving the guard next to it in one go.
analogies.city: Think of a mayor moving behind the city wall while a guard takes his place beside him.
analogies.farm: The farmer steps into the barn, and the sheepdog jumps beside him, both in one move.
analogies.sport: Like a goalkeeper and a defender swapping places quickly to protect the goal.

stages.mnemonic: Castle: king two steps, rook hops over. En passant: capture right now or never.

Kingside

stages.title: Pawn promotion
stages.hook: A tiny pawn can walk all the way across the board and change into something much stronger. What do you think it becomes?
explain: When a pawn reaches the far end of the board, the last rank, it must promote. The player replaces it with a queen, rook, bishop or knight of the same colour. It cannot stay a pawn, and it cannot become a king.

Most players choose a queen, because it is the strongest piece. So you can have two or more queens on the board! Choosing a knight, rook or bishop is called underpromotion. It is rare, but sometimes it is better: a knight can give a check that a queen cannot, or it can avoid a stalemate.
A pawn that is close to promoting is a big danger, so the other side must stop it. In notation, promotion is written like a8=Q.

example.q: A white pawn is on a7 and the square a8 is empty. Black has a king on h8 and nothing else on the a8-h8 line. What happens after a8=Q?
steps: The pawn reaches the last rank and is replaced by a queen.
The new queen on a8 looks along the 8th rank to h8.
It gives check, written a8=Q+.

analogies.home: It is like a child reaching the top of the school and becoming a prefect.
analogies.city: A messenger who reaches the capital is promoted to a minister.
analogies.farm: A seedling that reaches the top of the field becomes a tall plant.
analogies.sport: A young player who scores in the last minute is named captain.

stages.mnemonic: Pawn walks to rank eight, then it gets a crown.

panel.q: What could go wrong if you always promote to a queen?
panel.model: A queen can create a stalemate in some endings, and in rare cases a knight gives a winning check or fork a queen cannot.
panel.why: Sometimes a lower piece wins where a queen does not.

stages.title: Opening principles
stages.hook: In the first ten moves of a chess game, what should you be trying to do? Run for the king? Or something slower?
explain: The opening is the first stage of the game. Good habits help: control the centre, develop your pieces, and make your king safe. Do not move the same piece again and again for no reason, and do not bring the queen out too early because it can be chased.
Moving pawns such as e4 or d4 take central squares and open lines for bishops and the queen. Then bring out knights and bishops. Then castle.
Each move should have a purpose. Do not make moves just to move. A good opening gives you a plan for the middle of the game.

example.q: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4. Which opening principles does White follow?
steps: e4 takes the centre.
Nf3 and Bc4 develop a knight and a bishop.
The pieces also prepare for castling.
example.a: Centre, development, and getting ready to castle

analogies.home: Before you cook, you set the table and bring out the pots. The opening is that preparation.
analogies.city: A city builds roads and a centre first, before it builds the far districts.
analogies.farm: You prepare the field and fetch your tools before you plant.
analogies.sport: In football, you spread to your positions before attacking.

stages.mnemonic: Centre, Develop, Castle: C-D-C. Do not rush the queen.

Development

Tempo

questions.model: Each move should add a new piece to the game. Moving the same piece again wastes time while the opponent brings out more pieces.
questions.why: The player who develops faster gets more activity.

questions.q: Which sequence follows the principles best?
questions.why: It controls the centre, develops, and castles.

To make sure the opponent castles first

The queen is trapped and cannot move at all

panel.why: Minor pieces can attack the queen and gain tempi.

panel.q: Why is the centre important?
panel.model: Pieces in the centre can reach more squares, so they control more of the board.
panel.why: A piece on the edge has far fewer moves.

panel.q: If both players follow all the principles, what usually follows?
o: A forced win for the side with the first move
An immediate stalemate on the next move
A draw agreed at move five
panel.why: Principles help but do not guarantee a win.

teach.model: In the opening: take the centre, develop knights and bishops, and castle to protect the king. Avoid moving one piece many times or bringing the queen out too early.

points.ask: How do I look after my king?

stages.title: Piece development
stages.hook: Your knight sits at home on g1, hidden behind a pawn. Is it helping you? What if it jumps out?
explain: Developing a piece means moving it from its home square to a place where it does more. Knights usually come out first, to squares like f3 and c3. They look towards the centre. A knight on the edge sees few squares, which is why people say: "a knight on the rim is dim".
Bishops come out next. A pawn move such as e4 or d4 opens a diagonal for a bishop. Place bishops on open diagonals where they can see many squares.
After that, castle, and then connect your rooks so they can protect each other along the first rank. Try to move each piece only once or twice in the opening.

example.q: After 1.e4 e5, which is the better development: 2.Nf3 or 2.Na3?
steps: Nf3 goes towards the centre and attacks the e5 pawn.
Na3 puts the knight on the edge, where it controls few squares.
So 2.Nf3 is the better development.

analogies.home: You take toys out of the box so you can play with them. Pieces at home are not playing.
analogies.city: A fire engine in the garage cannot help. It must go out to the street.
analogies.farm: A sheepdog tied to the fence cannot herd. It must be near the flock.
analogies.sport: A substitute on the bench does not help the team until he comes on to the pitch.

stages.mnemonic: Knights before bishops, then castle, then connect.
terms: Development
Moving a piece off its start square to a useful one.
Open diagonal
A diagonal with no blocking pawns, good for a bishop.
Connect the rooks

misc.wrong: A knight on the edge is as strong as one in the centre.
misc.right: A knight in the centre reaches 8 squares, but on the edge only 4 or fewer.

o: The other pieces stay at home, so you fall behind

panel.why: Bishops need open diagonals now; rooks need open files later.

panel.q: Why is a lead in development an advantage?

teach.model: Developing means bringing pieces to active squares. Knights go towards the centre, bishops go to open diagonals, then castle and connect the rooks. A knight on the edge sees little.

stages.title: Control of the centre
stages.hook: Four squares in the middle of the board: d4, e4, d5 and e5. Why do chess players fight over them?
explain: The centre is the four squares d4, e4, d5 and e5, with the squares around them. A piece in the centre can reach more squares than a piece on the edge. It can quickly go to either side of the board.
You can control the centre in two ways. You can put pawns there (e4, d4), which also attack nearby squares. Or you can attack the centre from a distance with pieces like bishops and knights.
The centre also helps your attack and defence. If you have more control there, your opponent has less room to move.

example.q: A knight on d4 and one on a1. Which attacks more squares?
steps: The knight on d4 has 8 jumps.
The knight on a1 is in a corner with only 2 jumps (b3 and c2).
The central knight is much stronger.
example.a: The knight on d4 attacks 8 squares, the one on a1 only 2

analogies.home: The living room is the middle of the house: from there, you can reach every room fast.
analogies.city: A central station connects many roads. A station on the edge connects few.
analogies.farm: A well in the middle of the farm can serve every field.
analogies.sport: In basketball and football, the centre of the pitch is where the game flows.

stages.mnemonic: Centre squares: d4, e4, d5, e5. From the middle, go everywhere.
terms: Centre
d4, e4, d5, e5, the four middle squares.
Occupy
To put a piece or pawn on a square.
Control
To attack a square so the opponent cannot use it safely.

misc.wrong: The centre only matters in the opening.
misc.right: Control of the centre helps all through the game, though the plan can change.

panel.why: A pawn centre can become a target.

stages.title: King safety
stages.hook: In a battle, the leader is protected carefully. In chess, what protects the king?
explain: The king is the one piece you cannot afford to lose. In the opening and middle game the king is safest in a corner, behind pawns. Castling gets the king there fast.
Pawns in front of the king act like a wall. If you move the pawns in front of your castled king, you make holes that an attacker can use. Keep a pawn shield of three pawns.

A common danger is the back rank. If the king is behind its pawns and the first rank is empty of defenders, a rook or queen can checkmate on the back rank. A small pawn move such as h3, called "luft", gives the king an escape square. In the endgame the king becomes active and should come to the centre.

example.q: White king e1, rook a1, Black king g8 with pawns f7, g7, h7. White to move. What is the best move?
steps: The black king has no escape squares because his own pawns block the 7th rank.
Ra8 gives check along the 8th rank.
Nothing can block or capture, so it is checkmate: Ra8#.

stages.title: Basic chess tactics
stages.hook: A good chess player often wins a piece with a single clever move. How can one move attack two things at once?
explain: A tactic is a short plan that wins material or checkmates. Tactics begin with seeing what is attacked and what is not protected. A piece that nobody protects is "hanging". Before every move, ask: what is my opponent threatening, and what can I attack?

A fork is when one piece attacks two or more enemy pieces at the same time. Knights are great forkers because they attack in an L shape that few pieces can guard against. A pin is when a piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it. A skewer is like a pin the other way round: the valuable piece must move and the piece behind it is captured.
The best way to improve is to check three things on every move: checks, captures and threats. Then check what the opponent could do in reply.

example.q: White knight on d5, Black king on e8, Black rook on a8. White to move. What wins a rook?
steps: Look for a knight move that attacks the king and the rook together.
Nc7+ attacks e8 and a8 from c7.
The king must deal with the check, so White takes the rook next: Nxa8.

stages.title: Elementary logical reasoning
stages.hook: Three friends each hold a different chess piece. You get three clues. Can you work out who has what, without guessing?
explain: Logical reasoning means getting a certain conclusion from facts. If the facts are true and the reasoning is right, the answer must be true. We call this deduction.

An "if... then..." statement links two facts. If a piece is a bishop, then it moves on diagonals. A piece moves in an L. Is it a bishop? No. The facts allow only a knight. Be careful: "if bishop then diagonal" does not mean "if diagonal then bishop", because a queen also moves on diagonals.

Another tool is elimination: cross out what cannot be true until one answer is left. Chess uses the same thinking: "If he takes my knight, then I take his rook. If he does not, then I fork his pieces."

example.q: Mia, Noor and Omar each hold one piece: king, queen or rook. Noor has the queen. Mia does not have the king. Who has the king?
steps: Noor has the queen.
Mia cannot have the king, so she must have the rook (the queen is taken).
The king is left for Omar.
